title: The Power of Stories
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reflects on how engaging with stories and narratives can shape our experiences and perceptions, and encourages us to be mindful of our own storytelling in order to cultivate freedom and compassion. By recognizing the power of stories to influence us, we can choose to tell more expansive and hopeful narratives that bring us closer to reality and each other. This involves approaching life with a sense of openness and awareness, cutting through layers of meaning and conditioning to reveal a more authentic and compassionate way of being.

sentences.text: Good morning.
Hi everybody, good to be speaking with you tonight.
I think I've touched base with most everybody on the screen since I returned from sabbatical, but if not, good to see you again.
I don't think I've given a talk until now, though.
First I want to really thank our wonderful speakers in July while I was away.
If you didn't hear those talks, I really highly recommend listening to them on the website, and I can give you a little teaser here to motivate you.
Talus led off with a great talk called "Oops," or something like that, about the incredible value of our mistakes.
How else do we ever learn anything?
Dogen is often quoted as saying that life is one continuous mistake, but I've never been able to find that anywhere in his writings, so that's just what people say, but it's probably true.
One continuous mistake.
Oops.
And Chris, who's on her way to Germany, I think at this very second, maybe she's still in the air.
She shared some great stories about Ananda, the Buddha's longtime attendant and his cousin, who famously remembered all of his Dharma talks and would repeat them for the monks.
I really enjoyed hearing Chris's appreciation of Ananda because he's always been a favorite of mine.
I love how in the stories he is portrayed as so earnest and so devoted, always working hard on his practice, but he never can quite get it.
Can't you relate to that?
But of course, at the end, their stories are told in this kind of dualistic way, like they're not enlightened and then they are enlightened.
So in the end he wakes up, but only after the Buddha passes away, because all the monks were going to review all the teachings.
They hope he'll come to this meeting to review all the teaching, because he's the one who remembers them all.
But at this meeting only enlightened people are allowed.
So he'd better get enlightened, so that night he does.
It's great.
Thank you, Ananda, for telling us all the teachings and for your hard work in your practice.
And Chris also told the story of Ananda going to bat for women as serious practitioners with the Buddha.
And then Bob Penny shared a powerful talk about how the world is burning, and yet the world is our teaching.
He used the wonderful koan, which I'd forgotten about, but it's such a powerful koan.
It's in the Blue Cliff Record, thirty-something.
The whole koan is a quotation.
*Medicine and sickness heal each other.
The whole world is medicine.
Where do you find yourself?*
*Medicine and sickness heal each other.
The whole world is medicine.
Where do you find yourself?*
Where indeed?
And then John encouraged our continuous practice in his usual practical, grounded, wise way.
Always such a pleasure.
How we just keep going.
We just keep appreciating this life, this practice, which is the same thing.
And I love how he really emphasized how essential it is for us to keep showing up and reminding ourselves to show up, reminding each other to show up.
Showing up again and again and again on the cushion, in the Zoom zendo, in our lives, with patience and forbearance and trust.
John always finds great quotations.
There was a nice quotation from Mel Weitsman, some stuff that Merle said during a sesshin one time.
The kind of quotation we shouldn't read too often because it makes a sesshin sound really hard, and really, really painful and stuff, but also beautiful, very beautiful.
So anyway, here we are.
We just go on, right, together, trying to encourage each other to stay on the beam, to keep practicing, to help as we can.
The world sure seems to be in all kinds of trouble.
And yet the future is as unknowable as it ever was.
We think we know what's going to happen, right, but we know it's not really true.
It's not really knowable.
And of course, right now it's distressing because we probably all thought we'd be wrapping up with COVID about now, but the disease didn't hang around and wait for us.
It went ahead and mutated.
Now things are complicated. [unclear: "I'll go over again"].
And while we're on that topic, I just want to mention that the practice committee met a couple of days ago to discuss our possible return to offering an in-person option for the Wednesday night sit.
We're tentatively planning for September 15th.
So I just wanted you to know what we've decided, and that we've also decided that we can't decide.
And this will come out in the wonderful newsletter.
Thank you, communications committee.
Really great newsletter.
This last one was beautiful.
Anyway, we decided about Wednesday night practice in person.
Well, first, if infections continue to rise, we'll probably just postpone.
And when we do get to practice, we're going to rent the Shambhala Center on Meridian across from the Haggen there.
And we thought we'd do it this way, just so you have a little picture in your head.

Each person who comes would sign in below at the front door and put their signature to an attestation that they are fully vaccinated, and put their contact info so we could do contact tracing if something happens.
We're not going to check your immunization card.
We decided that we're going to have people say, "Yes, I'm vaccinated," and sign.
There is unfortunately a flight of stairs up to their space.
Not like an endless flight of stairs like a couple of Dharma halls ago, but there's a flight of stairs, unfortunately, and no elevator.
So not a perfect solution.
We'll stay masked the whole time and we'll go ahead and do our whole form with bells and bows and chanting.
Although I think we'll be mindful to not really blast out the chanting.
We'll chant softly to reduce the risk and keep it mellow.
And there's a pretty big place there.
We'll distance as reasonable.
Probably we can do regular social distancing because we don't expect very large numbers after I say all this.
Like who would want to go?
But it sure will be a wonderful day to practice again.
Maybe it'll end up being like the doanryo.
Or sometimes the doanryo and other times [unclear: "I'll be through this"].
We'll see.
It's all unknown.
And Shambhala assures us they have really good internet, so we can broadcast the Zoom from there.
In fact, their main practices have been broadcast to me the whole time, it turns out.
So you can still tune in on Zoom.
So anyway, stay tuned.
See what actually happens, but that's what we're thinking.
Oh, and it's also very nice: Shambhala is offering us a really reasonable rental rate and a lot of flexibility.
We're not locked into anything, and we'll just pay for what we actually use.
And maybe later in the fall, who knows, we'll also add Saturday morning practice there.
And I told Robin from Shambhala that we include cleaning in our practice.
And it's very sweet.
He said, "Oh, well, don't pay us an hourly rate to clean our building.
Take that off."
That's nice.
Anyway, stay tuned.
Thank goodness for this way of being together, huh?
So I don't know about you, but lately I've been really noticing and feeling into times when I feel really stuck in myself.
Do you know what I mean?
I feel narrow, pinched, worried, anxious.
But other times, I don't feel that way at all.
I feel really open, expansive, trusting, happy.
And it comes and goes.
And it's a big simplification to say that there's just two states, but it's been seeming that way to me lately.
A narrow state and a wide state.
And of course, I prefer the latter to the former.
And of course, there's a part of me that wishes I could always feel open, expansive, trusting, happy.
That's nice.
So it makes me wonder, as a conditioned being, well, how do I get more of that?
And since I have all this access to all this elaborate language and spiritual technology, then I'm thinking, oh, what are the best practices?
What are the right conditions to be that more open way?
But of course, then the next thought I have, unfortunately, is that conditions are mostly out of my control.
Almost all of them.

So isn't it a bit foolish to think that I can actually control my internal state, since everything that's happening with me in the conditioned world, like these mind states, is totally hinged and hooked on all the conditions that are influencing and affecting me, whatever "me" is?
So where's the real freedom here?
Is it somehow sort of gaming the system so I'll always feel good, or at least most of the time feel good, or more often feel good?
Or is the freedom allowing so-called good and bad to come and go, to arise and fall, to change in its own pattern and rhythm?
So how is it for you?
Are there times you feel tight and narrow, and other times you feel open and expansive?
What seems to help?
I use this language advisedly like "help."
And even though we can't really control all this, it definitely seems like it's skillful to notice what helps and choose that when we can.
We don't need to suffer any more than we have to.
And especially because we're so much more available to others, right?
We're more helpful to this world, this world that is medicine, and we can be medicine too, when we're more open, trusting and available, not pinched and narrow.
So it's not just for us.
It's part of our work as bodhisattvas, it's part of our vow.
Well, I noticed one thing that seems to help me recently, I kind of re-noticed this recently.
I notice a big shift sometimes when I enter into a fictional world.
I've been noticing, anew, the way the arts can be so helpful.
The arts aren't just sort of an extra.
They're an essential way for humans to explore their humanness.
And I notice this most obviously when I'm immersed in narrative arts: books, movies, quality shows.
And in this case, I noticed this softening and opening and release when I've been reading this novel.
I've actually been reading a novel for the first time in I can't think how long.
It's a wonderful new novel called *Damnation Spring*.
I forgot the author right now.
It's about a logging community in the north coast of California, the land of the redwoods, which is an area I know pretty well.
And it's set in the 1970s, just as the last of the privately owned old growth redwood is being cut down, which was massively profitable.
And this book is a really sympathetic and wise immersion into that world, and especially into the world of a few timber families and the local and only logging company they all work for.
It's an amazing book.
These people are strong and kind and confused and hard, hard workers.
Oh my gosh, so hard work.
And limited, delusional, sometimes prejudiced, in deep and believable ways.
These are really real people.
And the writing itself is also wonderfully spare and efficient.
I really admire the writing.
I really recommend this book, *Damnation Spring*.

But my point being that, lately for me, hanging out in Colleen and Rich Gunderson's little house along Damnation Creek, as they try to raise their son, make ends meet, inhabit the roles in their life that are so supportive and so limiting to them, work things out, make mistakes, it just totally melts me being there with them.
And it opens me up, makes me joyful and makes me sad, makes me root for them, makes me root for humanity and for the planet.
As Colleen suffered yet another miscarriage, I was so sad, horrible, horrible for her.
And Rich struggled to understand that and to be sympathetic, to express his love.

As the company boss tried to manipulate Rich into testifying that the chemical defoliant they were using to spray the brush, to get the brush down, is totally safe and no problem, trying to get the logger Rich to testify that the spray is totally safe.
And these two things are connected, of course.

I was just there with them, feeling the way the logging boss and Rich the logger are both in opposition to each other, opponents in the economic world that they're in, but also in total cooperation to keep this system working, keep the world afloat, keep things as they should go.
And then as Daniel Bywater struggles to bring his scientific expertise to bear, he's the kid who went off to college and came back, so few did in this community, these communities.
And he's trying to help his old neighbors, but he's also himself a Yurok Indian in days that are even more racist than ours.
You can just feel how he's both brilliant and patient and being so foolish, risking his life pushing the river to try to help these people who scorn him for the most part.
So really, he's been beautiful.
So I want to recommend, if you have lost track of literature like I had, find a good book, give yourself some time, or whatever other art form opens you up.
I noticed with this book that I have to be really mindful not to get greedy and read too much, because then I'm just sort of skimming the surface of their world.
I'm not really in their world.
I'm not reading it with full attention and full awareness and full immersion.
I have to show up for them as they show up for me.
But when I really can enter the story as fully as I can, there's this quality of opening to something bigger in my life that somehow this brilliant author has managed to channel.
And I feel different.
I feel better, opened up.
So I'm super grateful that I'm, I mean, I'm busy and everything.
I'm sure we're all busy, blah, blah, blah, but I can notice that I'm not so busy that I can't read.
What is it for you?
What opens you up?
Have you cried at a good movie lately?
There are so many ways that the story opens us up and helps us heal.
And this makes total sense really, doesn't it?
Because humans have been telling stories and listening to stories and living in stories for as long as we could talk, for as long as we've had language.
We've been immersed in story.
And then really, I think most of our interactions, even the little ones, are actually in the realm of story.
Even when we think we're talking about logistics and externals and direct practical things, I think we're actually telling ourselves and telling each other a lot of stories.
And stories can also create suffering, too, of course.
We tell and believe in stories that bind us into beliefs and assumptions about things that are often much more negative, much worse, much more narrow, limited, bigoted than they need to be.
Than they need to be.
So the stories that we tell and live in are the whole thing.
They're good and they're bad.
They're the burning world and they're the medicine.
The stories we tell are actually creating the world in a certain way.
Some would say the world is nothing but a story.
But this is not to deny the apparent concrete world that's out there.
Not to deny that new UN study that just came out about climate change.
I could barely get myself to do more than read the headline and the summary: that the whole world on average is already up at least two degrees Fahrenheit as a result of human activity.
It's certainly going to go higher, and now it's just a question of the choices we make, how high it will go.
But there's a little optimism in that, if you've heard about it.
The authors say we really could avert the worst disasters.
That is still possible.
So maybe that's an external reality, right?
Or is it a story?
Or both?
But regardless of the reality of the external world, how we respond and live in the world is so driven by stories, right?
The stories we tell each other, the stories we tell ourselves.
Like the case of climate change, the story that nothing can be done absolutely means nothing will be done.
Maybe a hopeful story is a story of denial.
Or maybe a hopeful story is a story of wise encouragement.
And if we're telling the story that something can be done, something will be done.
The more you think about this, the more you recognize we're just swimming in stories all the time.
It's amazing that we can actually communicate, because often when we're talking or communicating with someone else, we're telling a different story than they are.
Or there are multiple simultaneous layers of story, and we're focused on one and they're focused on a different one.
And yet somehow we muddle along as our stories shift and change and overlap, collapse and are recreated.
All this makes me think of a favorite koan, Case 16 from the Book of Serenity.
Here's the case.
*Dijon asked Xuishan, "Where do you come from?"
Xuishan said, "From the south."
Dijon said, "How is Buddhism in the south these days?"
Xuishan said, "There are extensive discussions."
Dijon said, "How can that compare to me planting the fields and making rice to eat?"
Xuishan said, "What can you do about the world?"
And Dijon said, "What do you call the world?"*
So the frame story here is assumed to be that Xuishan is a traveling monk.
In China you train somewhere for a while and then you travel, usually in the off season, to other monasteries, or maybe you're relocating.
Anyway, he's a traveling monk and he's just shown up at Dijon's monastery.
I like to assume that Dijon is not sitting on his abbot's seat inside but is out in the monastery gardens, working the fields, maybe down by the road.
And this new monk walks up.
So the teacher asks him, "Where are you from?"
And this could of course be seen as a practical question, which we believe not to be a story, maybe.
Where are you from on the planet?
But there's also a story here, a story question.
What is your story?
Where are you coming from?
How do you think about who you are?
What's your story?
Right?
It's another way to translate "Where do you come from?": "What's your story?"
And so the monk Xuishan rests for a moment on his walking staff and answers.
Maybe he knows or maybe he doesn't know that this is the abbot of the monastery.
The custom was to wear simple clothes, especially at work period.
Maybe it's like Norman Fischer's famous story of when he first ever met his teacher, Sojun Mel Weitsman.
Mel was working in the garden and Norman assumed he was the gardener, and the teacher would be in some lofty place inside.
It's a great Zen story.
I don't know if you've ever heard Norman tell that story.
The other little part of that great little story is that Norman asked Mel, "Is there a roshi here?"
He'd read in some book about roshis.
And Mel said, "No, no, there's no roshi.
There's only a priest," meaning himself.
But he didn't give that away.
Great story.
But anyway, back to our story.
Maybe he knew.
Who knows?
So Xuishan, the student, answers in a simple way: "I'm from the south."
And Dijon, the teacher, is apparently not satisfied with this answer.
So he asks a follow-up question: "How is Buddhism in the south these days?"
Which again has many layers of possible meaning, many stories.
How is practice there?
How is your practice?
What is it for you to be from the south?
What's your story?
There are so many layers of meaning in these koan stories.
But isn't that true of our everyday conversations too?
Only we're usually paying attention to one layer.
Like I was saying, sometimes our conversation partners pay attention to a different layer.
So there are always so many layers to us.
So Xuishan's answer to this insistence from the teacher, like "Tell me your story," is interesting.
He says, "There are extensive discussions."
In other words, there are a lot of stories.
I don't know where to start, teacher.
Stories about me, you, life, practice.
There are extensive discussions.
And then Dijon's answer to this is a cut-through.
The cut-through of storytelling is the way it's usually interpreted.
This is called a cutting phrase, a beautiful, powerful statement: "How can you compare that to me here planting the fields and making rice to eat?"
At first it does sound like a very powerful way to cut off all stories.
I'm practical.
I'm not involved in story.
I am growing rice to eat.
I'm in the real world.
But actually, it's a bit of a bait and switch, or a switching bait, what do you call that?
Because that's a story too, actually.
So it's maybe like a test.
And Xuishan, the monk, misses that.
He doesn't notice that the teacher's just telling another story.
So he asks the teacher the biggest question he could think of about this world of stories: "What can you do about the world?"
What is this world?
And then the final line is the teacher answering, and this line itself is what you'd always practice with in the koan.
The teacher answers, "What do you call the world?"
It's a good question for us to ask every day, I think.
What do you call the world?
What are you calling the world right now?
What story are you telling yourself?
What stories about yourself?
Stories about your loved ones?
Stories about everyone you encounter?
Stories about the way it all works or the way it's all supposed to work?
Stories about the future?
Stories about the past?
Even our so-called being in the present is being in a story of the present.
So what's worth pondering, I think, is life in a sea of stories.
Not that we can ever exactly leave the sea.
We're swimming.
We don't want to drown.
But it's better for us, I think, and better for all beings, if we know that it's just a story.
This helps us to open up.
Well, another story for us is the story of Red Cedar.
That story used to be the story of a small sitting group in library rooms and therapist meeting rooms.
And then there was the story of a couple of shared dharma halls, and the little group got a little bit bigger.
And then there's a story of this whole weird set of coincidences and this odd donation.
And then this little group got a little bigger and took out their first lease on a property, in 2007 is my story of when that was, on Forest Street.
And now there's a story here of somehow that group.
I always flinch a little bit when someone says, "What does the Sangha think?"
What does that mean?
That's another story.
The Sangha.
Who's that?
Is that you?
Is that me?
What if we think different things?
What if we have different stories?
And yet there's this thing, the Sangha.
That's our story.
So now somehow this Sangha story is on a screen.
It would have been unimaginable in the previous rounds of story making.
What if you went to a meeting and said, "Let's do this Zen thing through our computers"?
Anyway, now there's the new story, a very new, compelling story.
We're really interested in this story.
It's a very exciting story, this new story of raising money and buying property.
Of course, property ownership itself is a very powerful story.
A story that here can protect us as an organization.
Wonderful.
But also a story that has caused untold harm in the world, too, right?
The story of property ownership is also the story of displacement of the original inhabitants of this place, who of course are still here.
But that's another story.
Here, but suffering.
So anyway, I thought I'd tell you a little bit of this current story.
Some stuff we'll find out a little bit later.
It's all revving up.
The story's getting really hot and heavy.
It's a romance.
Very steamy.
So the story now is that we'll officially start asking for donations for the Capital Campaign in the middle of September.
And all this is, probably, a story.

There will be a beautiful brochure to read and other nice written materials, and they'll all lay out how it all works and why we're doing it and what our intention is, which we hope to tell a very good story about.
Very compelling.

And it'll tell the story of how each of us, and all of our other friends and supporters, can contribute to this new story of a Zen center that owns a physical space, a Zen community that can put down deeper roots and, we hope, be of stronger and more powerful service in the world.
The goal of the campaign, here's an astonishing story, is to raise $550,000.
This is astonishing to me both because it's a big number and because a couple of groups of us have worked carefully over months doing research, talking to people, assessing things.
And it's a number that we actually have confidence in.
Wild.
It's a true story.
Over half a million dollars.
Somehow it's going to work.
That's our story.
And we've already found a few possible properties.
I don't want to say too much about those stories because that's very much in flux.
Properties come and go.
So that's the story there.
May our dreams come true.
And lastly, before we close the formal talk, I just want to mention my intentions for the Wednesday evening Dharma talks coming up.
I thought, starting in mid-September, I'd like to start exploring with you the wonderful stories and teachings of the Lotus Sutra.
I've been enjoying Gene Reeve's translation after it sat on my shelf for I don't know how long, a decade.
But I've especially been enjoying it in combination with Thich Nhat Hanh's wonderful commentary on the Lotus Sutra, which is called *Peaceful Action, Open Heart*.
And I'll try to do it like I did with the Brain Science, where if you just show up it should still be interesting and valuable, but even more valuable if you read one or both books along with me.
You could actually read the text of the Sutra, but it does, I want to warn you, get a little convoluted.
And I'm going to try to do a little bit of organizing and clarifying the wonderful richness of this extravagant Sutra in the talks.
So if you don't have that kind of time, which would be great, but if you don't, the Thich Nhat Hanh book is quite a bit shorter and more accessible.
And it stands on its own pretty well, especially, hopefully, with the talks, where I'll try to fill in the story of the Sutra a little more that he's commenting on.
Various of us have taken stabs at this wonderful Sutra over the years, but I don't think we've ever done a thorough treatment of it as a whole Sangha.
Not that I'll read every word out loud with you, that would take probably multiple years.
We'll condense and summarize a bit, but read passages and sections and commentaries to really get a feeling for this.
Because the meaning is not just in the words, as one of our chants says.
It's also in the feeling and spirit of the text, which is pretty far out sometimes on purpose.
So even that, though, will take a while.
I don't know how long.
I spent a couple of years in the Mumun Khan, so I don't know, it'll be like that.
I don't know.
But what's wrong with that?
Do you have a story that we're supposed to go at any particular pace and talk about any particular thing in the Dharma talks?
Should each one be some one-off neat little useful teaching?
I don't know.
So anyway, that's the story of future talks.
We'll still have the precept ceremony on the first Wednesday of the month.
And I think while the fundraising story is hot and heavy, we'll have that Sangha conversation, discussion, presentation-y time on the last Wednesday.
So that drops a few weeks out from the talks.
Anyway, I'll try to get all that info about the Lotus Sutra and the talk series on the website and the wonderful new newsletter.
But the key thing is just to remember the title of Thich Nhat Hanh's book, or just wait till it shows up in your inbox.
The book is called *Peaceful Action, Open Heart*.
I wish they wouldn't do poetic titles for his books, because you can never remember which ones are which.
**Participant:** Hey, Tim, I have a question about that.
I have his commentary, but it's an older version and it's called *Opening the Heart of the Cosmos*.
Or something.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** I think it's the same because they haven't changed the poetic titles, but I'll have to, yeah, I'll check in with you.
I'm sure it's the same thing.
It's his commentary on the Lotus Sutra, but it was called *Opening the Heart of the Cosmos*.
So if someone sees an old copy and thinks they're different, I don't think they are.
Sometimes they do an editing pass, just to tighten up mistakes and stuff.
But yeah, I bet it's basically the same.
Thanks, Desiree.
It's good to know.
Well, let's end the evening with a shorter koan, or at least the formal talk.
Here's Book of Serenity, case 27, which is called Fionn Points to a Blind, a blind like a window blind.
Here's the case.
*Fionn pointed to a blind.
Two monks went at the same time and rolled up the blind.
Fionn said, "One gain, one loss."*
*Fionn pointed to a blind.
Two monks went at the same time and rolled up the blind.
Fionn said, "One gain, one loss."*
There are a lot of rich stories there.
But wherever we go, right, there's gain and loss.
What else would we expect?
Thanks for listening to that as I fade into the darkness.
So I'll chant, let's chant out, and then see if you have a few things to say before we call it a night.
I hope you do.
*May our intention equally extend to every being in place with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless.
I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible.
I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless.
I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable.
I vow to become it.*

their stories are told in this kind of dualistic way, like they're not enlightened and then they are enlightened. So we will hope you come to this meeting to review all the teaching, because you're the one who remembers them all. But this meeting is only enlightened people are allowed. So you better get enlightened so that night he does. It's great. Thank you, Ananda, for telling us all the teachings and hard work in your practice.
